human-cell.title: Human Cell
human-cell.summary: Explore the microscopic anatomy of the human cell, including the nucleus, mitochondria, and cell membrane.
human-cell.focus: Cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria (ATP), endoplasmic reticulum, and ribosomes.

cues.text: Every human cell is completely enclosed by a flexible cell membrane. This lipid bilayer controls which essential nutrients enter and which waste products leave the cellular interior.
Inside lies the cytoplasm, a rich water-based jelly filling the entire interior cell space. Cellular organelles float safely in the cytoplasm, suspended and organized by fibrous protein structures.
Notice the circular human cell shape on our board: flexible and dynamic, unlike rigid plant cells with stiff cellulose cell walls and green chloroplasts.
At the center sits the nucleus, the master control center of the entire cell. It securely houses our DNA genetic instructions inside a protective double membrane equipped with nuclear pores.
Surrounding the nucleus are oval mitochondria, often called the powerhouses of the cell. Mitochondria use oxygen and glucose from food to generate chemical energy in the form of ATP.
The inner folded membrane of each mitochondrion, called cristae, creates vast surface area for chemical reactions. Active cells like muscle cells contain thousands of energetic mitochondria.
Look at the ribbon-like folded channels around the nucleus dotted with tiny dark specks. Which cellular organelle manufactures new proteins directly from genetic codes?
Pause here to trace the folded membranes. Think about how ribosomes and ER cooperate.
Those tiny specks are ribosomes, and the folded highway is the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Ribosomes read RNA copies from the nucleus and assemble chains of amino acids into proteins.
The Golgi apparatus then packages these finished proteins into vesicles for delivery throughout your body. Check: ribosomes build, the Golgi packages and ships.
All vital organelle systems work together in wonderful harmony: the nucleus instructs, mitochondria power, ribosomes build, and the flexible cell membrane protects.
Trillions of human cells specialize into nerve, muscle, bone, and skin cells while sharing these same fundamental organelle components.
Read the study notes to compare animal and plant cell structures, and ask your tutor any question about cellular respiration or protein synthesis.

notes.title: The nucleus commands and protects DNA
notes.text: The nucleus is enclosed by a double-layered nuclear envelope with pores regulating transport. Inside, DNA stores the master genetic blueprint for synthesizing all proteins required by the human body.

notes.title: Mitochondria generate cellular fuel
notes.text: Through cellular respiration, mitochondria break down glucose in the presence of oxygen to synthesize adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy currency utilized across all cellular metabolic processes.

notes.title: Protein production pipeline: Ribosomes to Golgi
notes.text: Ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum assemble amino acid chains. The synthesized proteins travel to the Golgi apparatus, where they undergo folding, biochemical modification, and vesicular packaging.

human-cell.mistake: Don’t confuse human cells with plant cells. Human cells possess flexible cell membranes and mitochondria, but do not contain rigid cellulose cell walls, large central vacuoles, or chloroplasts.

practice.question: Why do active muscle cells contain substantially higher concentrations of mitochondria than skin cells?
practice.answer: Muscle cells continuously contract and require high quantities of ATP energy, which mitochondria produce via aerobic cellular respiration to power muscular exertion.

trigonometry.title: Trigonometry & Right Triangles
trigonometry.summary: Master trigonometric ratios—sine, cosine, tangent (SOH-CAH-TOA)—and learn how to calculate unknown sides, angles, and real-world distances.
trigonometry.focus: Right-angled triangles, Hypotenuse, Opposite, Adjacent, Sine, Cosine, Tangent, and the Pythagorean Identity.

cues.text: Trigonometry begins with the right-angled triangle. One angle is exactly ninety degrees, and the longest side opposite to it is called the hypotenuse.
When we choose an acute reference angle theta, the other two sides gain specific names: the opposite side facing theta, and the adjacent side running alongside it.

Notice how changing which acute angle we observe swaps opposite and adjacent. The hypotenuse always remains fixed opposite the ninety-degree right angle, providing an unchanging anchor for all calculations.

chapters.title: The Primary Ratios: Sine and Cosine

cues.text: The sine ratio compares the opposite side to the hypotenuse: sine of theta equals opposite over hypotenuse. As theta grows, sine increases from zero up to one.
The cosine ratio compares the adjacent side to the hypotenuse: cosine of theta equals adjacent over hypotenuse. At zero degrees cosine is one, decreasing to zero at ninety degrees.
Together, sine and cosine determine the exact coordinates of any point on a unit circle, linking right-angle geometry to circular wave motion.

chapters.title: Tangent and the SOH-CAH-TOA Memory Tool

cues.text: The third ratio is tangent: tangent of theta equals opposite over adjacent. Tangent also represents the slope or steepness of the hypotenuse incline.
Think carefully: which legendary three-letter memory word unites all three fundamental trigonometric definitions on our board today?
Remember the famous acronym: S-O-H C-A-H T-O-A. Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse; Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse; Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent. It is the master memory tool of trigonometry.
With SOH-CAH-TOA, if you know just one side and one acute angle, you can calculate every missing dimension in the triangle.
Because opposite squared plus adjacent squared equals hypotenuse squared, dividing by hypotenuse squared reveals the fundamental identity: sine squared plus cosine squared always equals one.
Surveyors, astronomers, and navigation satellites use trigonometry every day to measure mountain heights, ocean distances, and orbital paths without physical measuring tapes.
Review the study notes on your board, and ask your tutor any question about angle calculations, inverse trig ratios, resolving missing sides, or real-world distance problem solving.

notes.title: The Core Trigonometric Ratios (SOH-CAH-TOA)
notes.text: For any acute angle θ in a right-angled triangle, the three primary ratios compare side lengths: Sine = Opposite / Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent / Hypotenuse, and Tangent = Opposite / Adjacent.
notes.equation: sin θ = Opp/Hyp · cos θ = Adj/Hyp · tan θ = Opp/Adj

notes.title: The Fundamental Pythagorean Identity
notes.text: Derived directly from the Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²), dividing all terms by the square of the hypotenuse yields the most famous identity in trigonometry: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.

notes.title: Special Right Triangle Exact Values
notes.text: 30°-60°-90° and 45°-45°-90° triangles produce exact ratio values: sin(30°) = 1/2, cos(30°) = √3/2, sin(45°) = √2/2, and tan(45°) = 1.

trigonometry.mistake: Don’t mix up Opposite and Adjacent when changing which angle you analyze. The Opposite side is strictly opposite angle θ, while Adjacent is the touching side that is not the hypotenuse.

practice.question: In a right triangle with angle θ, if Opposite = 3 and Hypotenuse = 5, what is sin(θ) and what is the Adjacent side length?
practice.answer: sin(θ) = 3/5 = 0.6. By Pythagoras (c² = a² + b²), Adjacent = √(5² - 3²) = √(25 - 9) = √16 = 4.
